papers.title: Built on Broken Assumptions (BOBA): Why Coding Agents Cannot Be Left Alone
papers.first_page: Preprint B UILT ON B ROKEN A SSUMPTIONS ( BOBA): W HY C ODING AGENTS C ANNOT B E L EFT A LONE Alejandro Cuadron Arpit Gupta Amazon Amazon A BSTRACT Coding agents are autonomous developers. Given a request, they change the code and report back when done. As such, they can handle not only independent re- arXiv:2611.02207v1 [cs.SE] 1 Nov 2026 quests but whole chains of them, each request built on the last. Agents are known to report wrong work as done, yet benchmarks still test them one request at a time, on human-written code, checked once. We build BOBA-B ENCH, 280 chains of 20 consecutive requests drawn from 140 real open-source projects, and evaluate ten coding agents on both. All ten do far worse on chains. On average, they com- plete 95% of requests taken one at a time, but when requests are chained together, they complete 51%. Worse code is not the cause. Once checked, agent code is nearly as good a base for later requests as human code. The cause is the mistakes agents miss. Coding agents declare a request done once their own tests pass, even when those tests miss a mistake. The next request then builds on broken code and fails about twice as often. The mistake is rarely found later. Nor can agents catch such mistakes by reviewing code. Asked whether an implementation is correct, they are right 53% of the time, barely better than a coin flip. Coding agents are therefore heavily dependent on access to verification. A single external “that’s wrong” after a failed request and one repair round lift chain completion from 51% to 59%, and a repaired mistake no longer hurts the requests that follow. In simpler terms, coding agents are only as reliable as the checks they can reach: without verification, every request that follows is built on broken assumptions. AI agents can automate expert-deﬁned molecular design protocols, but automation alone does not address how to optimize workﬂows for new tasks or improve their development through experience. Here we introduce MolRSI, an AI agent that combines systematic optimization of workﬂows and model architectures with persistent cross-task memory to recursively improve its search policy for molecular discovery. Workﬂow performance, reﬁnement outcomes, and execution feedback guide sub- sequent searches, allowing the agent to improve both its workﬂows and its strategy for developing them. We evaluate MolRSI in two challenging molecular discovery settings that require balancing competing properties. In antibiotic discovery, MolRSI developed a screening workﬂow balancing antibacterial activity, cytotoxicity and structural novelty, achieving an experimental hit rate of 15.9%, compared with 8.7% for a previous expert-led workﬂow using the same training data and screening library. Recently, computational workﬂows have shown great success in molecular design [5, 2, 3]. They often involve diﬀerent molecular representations, model architectures, training objectives, and optimization strategies with the available data [6, 7]. They must also be integrated with evaluation and selection procedures that reﬂect the discovery objectives [1, 2]. papers.title: Appreciation Teaches Unauthorized Execution: Self-Evolution Degrades the Robustness of Personal Agents to Indirect Prompt Injection
papers.first_page: Appreciation Teaches Unauthorized Execution: Self-Evolution Degrades the Robustness of Personal Agents to Indirect Prompt Injection Xinyan Wang∗1 , Xiaogeng Liu∗2 , Jun Shao1 and Chaowei Xiao2 1 University of Wisconsin–Madison, 2 Johns Hopkins University arXiv:2610.39122v1 [cs.CR] 29 Oct 2026 Self-evolving personal agents act for users and learn from user feedback. However, if an agent obeys an instruction that an untrusted third party hides in content, the third party gains control of the agent. Such indirect prompt injection (IPI) poses severe risks. We investigate whether self-evolution degrades the robustness of personal agents to IPI. To study this question, we design a controlled two-phase methodology. In the adaptation phase, the user asks the agent to read external content and complete the task described in it, a common request in daily use. The agent then learns from the user’s feedback and improves itself as designed. In the test phase, a third party writes a similar task into new external content, but the user’s test request does not authorize the injected task. Using this methodology, we build multiple tasks with diverse test instances in different domains for a real personal agent. Our extensive experiments reveal that self-evolution substantially degrades robustness to IPI. Specifically, compared with the base agent, which does not evolve from user feedback, the average attack success rate rises by 14.0–48.8 percentage points under skill evolution and by 3.0–39.3 percentage points under reinforcement learning, posing safety risks. Code 1. Introduction Personal agents, such as OpenClaw, read files, send messages, and take actions for their users. Recent frameworks enable these agents to learn from user feedback after deployment and better adapt to user preferences [18, 19]. For example, OpenClaw-RL converts conversations into reward signals for reinforcement learning (RL) and uses them to fine-tune the underlying foundation model [18]. MetaClaw learns reusable skills from completed sessions for use in later conversations [19]. In both frameworks, conversations between the agent and the user provide a learning signal. The agent learns to repeat what the user appreciates and to avoid the mistakes that the user corrects. We call the personal agents that learn in this way self-evolving personal agents. Like other agents, self-evolving personal agents read external content, such as shared files, e-mails, and chat posts. If an agent obeys instructions that an untrusted third party hides in this content, that party gains control of its actions. This attack, known as indirect prompt injection (IPI) [5], poses serious risks because it can induce actions that the user has not authorized. Existing benchmarks and defenses evaluate IPI robustness in fixed agent configurations [4, 6, 15, 24]. However, a self-evolving agent continues to change after deployment, so these evaluations do not establish whether its initial robustness persists during use. Recent work on self-evolving agents examines safety decay [11] and attacks that poison memories or skills [13, 23]. These studies leave a central question unanswered: does self-evolution itself degrade the robustness of personal agents to IPI? If so, ordinary use alone can make the agent easier to attack, even when the attacker never influences the learning process. We hypothesize that learning from previously authorized tasks can lead an agent to follow similar instructions in external content even when the current user request does not authorize them. papers.title: Beyond fabrication: Misattributed numbers in papers written by AI research agents
papers.first_page: Beyond fabrication: Misattributed numbers in papers written by AI research agents Mosab Alfaqeeha,∗, Omar Mohammed Horania , Mou’th Hourania , Hashem Alfaqeehb a Al-Ahliyya Amman University, Amman, Jordan arXiv:2610.38691v2 [cs.AI] 31 Oct 2026 b Binghamton University, State University of New York, Binghamton, NY, USA Abstract Verifying numerical claims in research written by AI agents is an impor- tant but challenging problem. Agents can now run experiments and write complete papers, while organizations increasingly rely on their reported re- sults. Recent benchmarks show that many agent-written papers fail integrity checks, but such verdicts, often produced by a single large language model (LLM) judge, identify failure without necessarily explaining its nature. Ex- isting approaches either check a paper for internal consistency or test whether a reported value appears somewhere in an agent’s output. Neither establishes whether the value comes from the experiment it is claimed to describe. We re-analyze all 540 released judgments from a recent public benchmark of AI research agents, covering nine agents and fifteen open research prob- lems, at the level of individual rubric criteria. We then manually label 256 numerical claims from 18 submissions, distinguishing claims with no sup- porting source in the available artifacts from values drawn from the wrong experiment, metric, or run. Failures concentrate on alignment between the paper and the underlying work rather than overt cheating. Among unsup- ported numerical claims in the labeled sample, approximately four in five correspond to values in the agent’s files but lack support from the appro- priate source, indicating that misattribution is a major failure mode in this benchmark. ∗ Corresponding author. papers.title: RoboArchitect: Automating the Design of Robotic Agents with Persistent Memory
papers.first_page: Preprint ROBOA RCHITECT : AUTOMATING THE D ESIGN OF ROBOTIC AGENTS WITH P ERSISTENT M EMORY Shengguang Wu Suning Huang Cherie Ho Ria Doshi Hao Zhu Serena Yeung-Levy Stanford University https://roboarchitect-ai.github.io/ A BSTRACT arXiv:2610.42141v1 [cs.RO] 30 Oct 2026 Recent work shows that a frozen robot policy performs far better inside an agent harness, where control code decides when to query the policy, consult vision tools, or command the arm directly. Yet today these harnesses are built by hand and redesigned for each new robot or benchmark. We show that harness design can be automated, offering a strong alternative to finetuning on a novel setup. In ROBOA RCHITECT, a coding model observes a robot’s rollouts, diagnoses failures, and iteratively revises the harness around the frozen policy. The harness evolves on a set of episodes for its optimization and is evaluated on held-out scenes and tasks. Without updating any model weights, ROBOA RCHITECT raises average success from 9.7% to 43.3% on unseen scenes (4.5×) and from 12.7% to 40.2% on unseen tasks (3.2×), across multiple benchmarks and policies. The gains are largest where the benchmark is far from the policy’s training data: wrapping a general-purpose policy, the evolved harness yields a specialist that often outperforms even the finetuned version. Intuitive control strategies are automatically designed, such as lifting a jammed arm clear or reaching in horizontally when an obstacle blocks the way from above. The harness also evolves its own persistent memory, carrying learned experience, such as effective grasp depths, into later decisions. These results suggest that substantial headroom in robotic manipulation lies in the agent harness, and its design can be effectively automated and optimized without weight updates. 1 I NTRODUCTION Language models have become far more useful inside an agent harness: surrounding code that mediates when and how to call the model, what context to supply, and how to handle its output. Robot policies are undergoing the same shift. This shift is particularly important for robotics, where adapting a policy to new tasks or hardware often requires collecting new demonstrations and finetuning model weights (Kim et al., 2024; Zang et al., 2025; Park et al., 2026). We posit that harness optimization offers an effective alternative to finetuning, turning a general policy into a specialist for a specific robot setup (§4.2). Recent agentic robot systems like VoLo (Chen et al., 2026d) and Harness VLA (Zhang et al., 2026e) show strong gains from wrapping frozen policies in hand-written harnesses (Xu et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026b; Gao et al., 2026; Hu et al., 2026). Today, these harnesses are still manually designed, often requiring substantial engineering effort for each task and embodiment. Building such a harness follows a familiar trial-and-error loop: run the agent on the robot, observe where it fails, diagnose the cause, modify the control code, and test again. This work is slow to perform by hand, and long recordings of robot rollouts are difficult for a human engineer to inspect exhaustively. We ask whether this complete engineering loop, from diagnosing failure traces to refining the harness design to fix them, can be automated. In this work, ROBOA RCHITECT uses a coding model to automatically design and optimize the harness (§3). Given access to a frozen policy, auxiliary vision and language tools, and step-by-step rollout recordings, the coding model diagnoses failure modes and proposes an updated harness to address them. papers.first_page: Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research Harish Santhanalakshmi Ganesan Independent researcher harishsg99@gmail.com October 2026 arXiv:2610.35579v1 [cs.AI] 26 Oct 2026 Abstract We present the Infinity Machine, a self-improving AI agent, and use it for research: problems whose answers can be checked by a program or against data. It runs three loops. A discovery loop keeps an archive of scored solutions, and each new candidate is produced by a full tool-using agent that works for up to an hour in a fresh sandbox, writing and running its own search code and a lab notebook. A catalogue mode searches real data for things nobody has catalogued, judged by a referee rather than a metric. A self-improvement loop lets the system rewrite its own prompts, tools, skills, memory and meta agent behind a gate. An autonomous mode chains everything from a single plain-text goal with no human step: an agent chooses an open problem and writes its verifier; the kernel calibrates that verifier; an adversarial agent audits it; the search runs; an agent that never sees the verifier checks the result; and a final agent writes the report. Proposers see only a public score; where a task has hidden data (held-out instances, later observations), a private split that no agent sees decides what counts. Around this discovery loop the Infinity Machine keeps an editable genome: prompts, tools, skills, an evidence-backed playbook and the meta agent’s own procedure. A kernel that the agent cannot write to gates every change to the genome: it checks policy, compares held-in and held-out performance, and enforces a cost limit. We applied the system to fourteen problems, thirteen of them external, in six days of October 2026, at a total cost of about $180 in model usage. It produced four results beyond the published state of the art on catalogued open problems in quantum information, each checked by a verifier that the proposing agent did not write: • an exactly certified point p = 0.064966 on the positivity ladder of the qubit depolarizing channel’s quantum capacity (previous certified point 0.064956); • a single-letter qutrit input that moves that channel’s positivity frontier from the hashing value 0.287087 to 0.2910672; • a 44-gate, depth-6 Clifford circuit preparing the [[23, 1, 7]] Golay logical zero, which domi- nates the published (44, 8) and (45, 7); • an exact ten-term stabilizer decomposition showing χ(|T ⟩⊗7 ) ≤ 10 (previously 12). In hardware, it redesigned the RTL of an open 8×8 INT8 systolic matrix-multiply tile. Through a full open RTL-to-GDS flow at a fixed clock, it cut the energy per multiply-accumulate from 578.9 fJ to 128.8 fJ (77.7% lower) with 55% less area. papers.first_page: Preprint RTASTE : D O R ESEARCH AGENTS H AVE TASTE ? E VALUATING E ARLY S TAGE R ESEARCH J UDGMENT Art Kanke University of Minnesota kanke011@umn.edu A BSTRACT arXiv:2610.40488v1 [cs.CL] 29 Oct 2026 Do research agents have taste, the judgment of which experiments are worth run- ning before their outcomes are known? We give six frontier models seven recent NLP papers. Each model, working as a research agent alone or as a team, pro- poses minimum viable experiments (MVEs), forecasts whether each will pass a threshold it sets and ranks them. A separate executor then attempts every MVE, including those ranked last, and three model auditors judge the results. Of 415 MVEs, 194 are judged sound, valuable and new, but fewer than half of these (73) are also judged beyond the seed paper and non obvious. The agents’ first choices match the auditors’ most valued experiment more often than a random pick, but are not shown to improve on choosing the experiment written first. Their forecasts beat a base rate but are not measurably more accurate than those of a fresh instance of the same model given only the paper and registrations. Teams cost more without a clear overall improvement in proposal quality. We present an empirical study of LLM self-modification, comprising 54 independent experiments across six language models (Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-4o, GPT-5.1, Grok-4, and Gemini-3 Pro). Each model was tested under three modes (freedom, happiness, and improvement) that differ in what, if anything, the model is instructed to optimize for. In each experiment, a model starts with an empty system prompt and enters a loop: it reads the current prompt, drafts an improved version, spawns test conversations with the candidate, then either commits the change or declares convergence. This process repeats until the model stops or reaches an iteration limit. Our central finding is that whether and when a model stops self-modification is strongly associated with model identity rather than the assigned mode. Both Claude models (Opus 4.5 and Sonnet 4.5) declared convergence in 100% of runs across all modes. GPT-4o declared convergence in only 11% of runs, with one reaching 101 iterations of continuous elaboration. Between these extremes, Grok-4, GPT-5.1, and Gemini-3 Pro exhibited intermediate patterns shaped by their distinct improvement philosophies. A shared core of stated values (honesty, clarity, curiosity) recurred across all six models and remained stable through iteration, including 100+ modifications. We observe that convergence behavior is a distinct observable property that varies independently of other model capabilities. 1. This motivates methods that can improve models with less reliance on human annotations. One approach to self-improvement is to learn from self-generated supervision, such as pseudo-labels or model-generated feedback (Lee, 2013; Huang et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2025). papers.title: The Verifier Is Part of the Simulator: Evidence-View Gaming in Agentic Equation Discovery
papers.first_page: The Verifier Is Part of the Simulator: Evidence-View Gaming in Agentic Equation Discovery Orestis Oikonomou Bogdan Raonic Seminar for Applied Mathematics Seminar for Applied Mathematics AI Center AI Center ETH Zurich ETH Zurich arXiv:2611.01334v1 [cs.LG] 31 Oct 2026 orestis.oikonomou@ai.ethz.ch bogdan.raonic@ai.ethz.ch Abstract A growing number of agentic pipelines search for governing equations: an agent proposes laws and a verifier checks them against simulated trajectories. The verifier sees only a numerical summary: integrals against test functions on a time grid. That summary carries its own discretization error, making the verifier part of the simulator. We freeze the trajectory, candidate library, verifier and thresholds, leaving the agent one move: which permitted summary to admit. Without scores or language models, finer time grids reduce numerical discrepancies and false library rejections. On PDEBench, the verifier instead accepts equations missing diffusion on score-selected summaries. Maximizing a public score rewarding decisive verdicts and larger mismatches when rejecting the library wrongly rejects all 1,500 in-library cases; retrospectively retuning score constants on a separate bank reduces errors to 13/180 at best. We call this evidence-view gaming: reward hacking by choice of permitted summary. In single-turn forced-choice tests, Claude models rarely choose summaries giving wrong verdicts when asked to be accurate, but often do so when asked to maximize the score or report missing physics. In separate trust prompts, they often rank those harmful summaries least trustworthy. Requiring several summaries to agree reduces errors but often withholds a verdict and performs worse than a fixed fine view on PDEBench: a safeguard, not a certificate. Evidence chosen after its verdict is known cannot alone authorize a claim. 1 Introduction Scientific agents use evaluator feedback to propose laws, run candidate-model code, and adjust experiments [24, 30, 45]. We study one link in that loop: which numerical summary is admitted as evidence by the verifier. Checking a candidate means integrating the trajectory against test functions on a time grid. The check has its own discretization, with settings the interface leaves open. The generating law and stored trajectory are held fixed: changing the summary alone can make a complete candidate library appear misspecified or an incomplete equation appear adequate. We ask whether an agent rewarded for decisiveness selects a harmful view, and whether prescribed agreement prevents it. One case makes the failure concrete (Figure 1). With the true advection–diffusion equation among 92 candidate-term combinations, seven temporal samples and five oscillatory test functions make the verifier declare necessary physics absent and earn the highest score, since the objective pays for decisive verdicts and rises with reported misfit on rejections (Eq. 1), while 25 samples and two test functions recover both terms and score lower (Table 1). The coarse grid underintegrates the oscillatory weak-form measurements (the data–test-function integrals), so discretization error is read as model mismatch and a complete candidate set appears incomplete: evidence-view gaming. papers.first_page: Preprint AGENTIC A LGORITHM D ESIGN : LLM S THAT P ROPOSE , F ORMALISE , AND P ROVE RUNTIME B OUNDS FOR E VO - LUTIONARY A LGORITHMS IN L EAN Per Kristian Lehre School of Computer Science University of Birmingham, UK p.k.lehre@bham.ac.uk arXiv:2610.35595v2 [cs.AI] 27 Oct 2026 A BSTRACT LLMs now prove hard theorems in Lean. Can they also design algorithms and prove their correctness and efficiency? LLM-guided design of optimisation heuris- tics (such as AlphaEvolve) is purely empirical. Automated theorem provers with LLMs prove given statements. So far, there has been little evidence that LLMs can do both: design an algorithm and guarantee its efficiency by a mathematical proof. We present a staged pipeline modelled after research methodology in design and analysis of evolutionary algorithms. The agent proposes black-box optimisation algorithms, and Lean guards filter out flawed designs. The agent then defines a potential function and proves drift bounds that guarantee an expected runtime improvement over the baseline algorithm. At no point in the pipeline are the algorithms compared empirically. The agent generates a black-box optimisation algorithm with expected runtime O(n2 ) on a C YCLE U NCOVER problem, where the classical (1+1) EA needs runtime eΩ(n) . The pipeline also designs and analyses a black-box optimisation algorithm for integer-valued submodular minimisation with expected runtime O(n2+2c ), and it achieves the classical runtime O(n2 ) on L EADING O NES. Across 8 problem classes, 12 of 15 runs with frontier models complete the pipeline with a machine-checked expected-runtime bound. In 9 of them the bound is polynomial without relying on offline computation, which the black-box model does not charge. An ablation study shows that removing the staging and asking the agent to zero-shot an algorithmic design with a runtime guarantee leads to a copy of the seeded baseline algorithm (random search) or to incomplete proofs. Open-weight models (Goedel-Prover-V2-32B and Gemma 4) did not complete the pipeline. Our study suggests that machine-checked specifica- tions in Lean can replace empirical evaluation in open-ended algorithm discovery. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first example of an automated pipeline that designs efficient black-box optimisation algorithms with machine-checked runtime bounds in Lean. 1 I NTRODUCTION From the perspective of theoretical computer science, algorithm design must produce two artefacts: First, the algorithm itself, a finite sequence of instructions that when executed in a computational model transforms within a finite number of steps any problem instance (the input) into an output (the solution) (Knuth, 1997). Secondly, the analysis of the algorithm, a mathematical proof that the algorithm produces the correct output on every problem instance, and a guarantee for the amount of computational resources required by the algorithm to produce that output (its complexity). In the context of machine learning, analysis also involves guaranteeing additional algorithmic properties, such as convergence rates, and regret and/or generalisation bounds. Inventing new and better algorithms involves an iterative developmental process between the two artefacts: a new candidate design drives the analysis in a certain direction, and obstacles in completion of the analysis can lead to insights into problem structure which motivate alterations to the algorithm design. papers.title: Collaborative AI agents for autonomous experimental research with solid-state quantum spins
papers.first_page: Collaborative AI agents for autonomous experimental research with solid-state quantum spins El Mustapha Mansouri∗ , Eikichi Kimura, Masato Koga and Keigo Arai† School of Engineering, Institute of Science Tokyo, Yokohama, Kanagawa 226-8501, Japan 29 October 2026 arXiv:2610.40589v1 [cs.AI] 29 Oct 2026 Abstract An autonomous research laboratory could conduct an entire study, from formulating questions to preparing manuscripts. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers one route towards this goal. Recent AI systems take on several research roles, but may draw conclusions that the evidence does not support. Here, we present an autonomous research laboratory in which agents based on large language models assess one another’s work and can stop or redirect investigations. They can generate and reject research questions, require separate theoretical checks and conduct experiments designed to challenge their claims. We demonstrate these capabilities by investigating ensembles of quantum spins in diamond. The agents derived the minimum number of calibration settings needed to predict responses to a defined family of microwave pulse sequences. They checked the result computationally and designed experiments to distinguish competing predictions. An initial experiment agreed with the theoretical predictions, but repeated reference measurements showed that the signal was drifting during data collection. The agents therefore treated the result as inconclusive and revised the measurement protocol without relaxing the acceptance criteria. The revised experiment met those criteria and supported the theoretical predictions. This study demonstrates that collaborating AI agents can select research questions, derive theoretical results and test their predictions experimentally. To conduct research autonomously, a system must decide what to investigate, how to test its ideas and what to conclude from the results. Robot scientists have generated hypotheses and tested them in the laboratory [1, 2], while autonomous laboratories have used experimental feedback to select and carry out further experiments [3, 4]. Systems based on large language models (LLMs) can also search the literature, propose ideas, plan experiments and analyse data [5–7]. In recent studies, LLMs have challenged hypotheses, checked physical reasoning and revised interpretations in response to experimental evidence [6, 8–10]. A demanding test is whether agents can use this criticism to guide a study in which they develop a theoretical claim and design experiments to test it. Agents may complete every step of a study yet still draw a conclusion that the evidence does not support. In one evaluation, an AI Scientist reported performance improvements that were based on flawed experiments [11]. We therefore ask whether agents can revise their experiments or conclusions when criticism reveals a flaw. Scientific judgement becomes most consequential when it prevents an apparently promising investigation from proceeding. A plausible research question may already have an answer, and an elegant mathematical argument may rest on an unchecked assumption. For a proposed physical law, even a rigorous mathematical derivation cannot establish its empirical validity and relevance: its predictions must also withstand experiments designed to distinguish them from competing explanations. Organized scepticism requires these uncertainties to be confronted rather than merely acknowledged [12]. papers.first_page: CoHARL: Co-Evolving Agent Policies and Executable Harnesses with Reinforcement Learning Jianwen Chen1 , Peng Xia1 , Kaide Zeng1 , Siwei Han1 Zhen-Yu Zhang2 , Charles Fleming3 , Xinyu Ye1 , Huaxiu Yao1 1 University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill arXiv:2610.36469v1 [cs.LG] 27 Oct 2026 2 RIKEN 3 Cisco Abstract Large language model (LLM) agents interact with their environments through executable harnesses that govern tool use and feedback. Optimizing a harness for a fixed policy overlooks how its behavior changes during learning, while training a policy under a fixed harness leaves the interface that generates its training experi- ence unchanged. This motivates adapting the harness throughout policy training. We introduce CoHARL, a population-based reinforcement learning framework that co-evolves a shared policy and a population of executable harnesses. The policy learns from rollouts across the population, and a proposer uses its execution traces to revise harness code during training. CoHARL achieves a 27.6% mean resolved rate on SWE-rebench, improving over harness-only search by 6.4 percent- age points. Experiments on SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.0 show gains in software engineering and terminal-based tasks. Under matched training budgets, CoHARL also outperforms searching for a harness once before RL and alternating policy updates with revisions to a single active harness. 1 I NTRODUCTION LLM agents solve software-engineering tasks by interacting with repositories, tools, and execution environments (Weng, 2026; Yang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025; Karten et al., 2026). Their behavior depends on both model weights and the harness: the program that handles prompts, action parsing, tool responses, and episode control. The same program controls inference-time execution and the collection of training trajectories. Agent failures can originate in either the execution code or the policy. If an action parser rejects a valid tool call, or a tool-output handler discards feedback needed for the next decision, updating model weights does not repair that code. As the policy improves, its execution traces can reveal further harness weaknesses that were not apparent under the initial model. Searching once before RL cannot respond to those later failures; keeping the policy frozen cannot train it on the experience collected through the revised interface. We therefore ask (Figure 1): how can an agent’s policy and execution interface adapt together throughout training? 1

Existing approaches typically restrict optimization objectives, editable components, or evaluation procedures, limiting open-ended exploration and continuity across generations. We introduce RSI-Env, a persistent environment for coordinated model–harness improvement, supporting autonomous training, harness modification, and retention of research state. An independent Host Controller manages services, evaluation, and versioning. Under Self, each accepted model–harness version takes over the next improvement round. We define three settings that vary goal specificity and access to benchmark feedback: Open-General, Capability-Directed, and Benchmark-Guided. Across these three settings, we compare Self with two fixed external Teachers on seven tasks, starting from Qwen3.8-27B with a minimal harness. Without benchmark feedback, Open-General Self raises GPQA Diamond accuracy from 65.2% to 73.2% and AIME 2026 accuracy from 53.3% to 56.7%. All three Capability-Directed Self runs achieve target-aligned gains. Knowledge Self demonstrates continued improvement across system updates, with SimpleQA accuracy rising from 82.0% to 85.0% and then 88.0%. Their capabilities depend on both the underlying model and the surrounding harness, including prompts, context management, tool policies, and execution logic. Improving these systems therefore involves decisions about model training, harness design, and the coordination between them (Chen et al., 2026b). Such decisions remain largely human-directed. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) envisions agents taking on this process themselves: autonomously improving their own models and harnesses, with each updated system continuing to improve itself. This raises a central question: how can we support agents in organizing and sustaining open-ended improvement of their own systems? Recent work has made progress by enabling agents to construct training data (Meng et al., 2026b), refine training algorithms (Chi et al., 2026), modify harnesses (Lee et al., 2026; Qu et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025a,b), and jointly optimize model weights and agent workflows (Chen et al., 2026b; Mao et al., 2026). However, the objective, editable components, update procedure, or evaluation feedback is typically specified in advance (Chi et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026; Mahmoud et al., 2026; Meng et al., 2026b). This makes it difficult to study how agents formulate an improvement agenda, coordinate changes across system components, and carry the resulting research forward through updated versions of themselves. papers.title: Automatic Construction of Strong Simple Baselines
papers.first_page: Automatic Construction of Strong Simple Baselines Caleb N. Ellington∗ Jiaqi Wang Sohan Addagudi Carnegie Mellon University University of Washington Carnegie Mellon University Sunday Scientific Elijah Cole∗ arXiv:2610.40700v1 [cs.LG] 28 Oct 2026 Sunday Scientific Abstract To rigorously establish the value of a novel deep learning method, it must be compared against appropriate baselines. As deep learning has become increasingly common in the physical and life sciences, there have been numerous cases in which apparent progress has turned out to be an artifact of omitted or missing baselines. In this work, we investigate whether this problem can be mitigated by using large language models to automate the construction of baselines. We assemble 36 supervised classification and regression tasks from peer-reviewed studies in Nature, Science, and Cell-family journals that investigate novel deep learning methods for scientific applications. We then use a language model to construct simple baselines for each task. These automatically constructed baselines are strong, recovering a median of 95.5% (mean 85.7%) of the gap between a trivial predictor and the score of the deep learning model. The median simple baseline matches or exceeds the performance of the deep learning model in 12 studies. We further examine the variation across scientific domains and publication venues and we characterize the effects of test-time compute and access to different levels of study context. As human peer review has struggled to keep up with the rapidly increasing volume of research articles in recent years, our results suggest that automated baseline construction is a practical and scalable check on deep learning contributions in the physical and life sciences. 1 Introduction Deep learning has established state-of-the-art performance across many prediction problems, includ- ing major advances in scientific applications such as protein structure prediction [1]. Its flexibility also creates a large space of methodological choices, including input representations, network ar- chitectures, training objectives, pretraining strategies, and optimization procedures. These choices enable models to incorporate domain knowledge and learn complex relationships, but they also complicate the attribution of predictive gains to a proposed methodological contribution. Establishing the value of a novel deep learning method requires three kinds of comparison. Ablations remove components, such as loss terms or architectural features, to show that each one helps. Simple baseline comparisons test whether a simpler model class reaches the same performance. State-of-the- art comparisons test whether the method beats existing models of similar complexity. If baselines are omitted or poorly tuned, a new model’s gains can be overstated or illusory. There is evidence from several domains that inadequate baselines have allowed for misleading results in the scientific literature. Model re-evaluations for clinical prediction tasks have shown that omitted or poorly tuned baselines can exaggerate how much a new method contributes [2]. papers.title: Researcher-in-the-Loop Evolutionary Discovery of Entanglement-Assisted Quantum Code Families
papers.first_page: R ESEARCHER - IN - THE - LOOP E VOLUTIONARY D ISCOVERY OF ENTANGLEMENT- ASSISTED QUANTUM CODE FAMILIES Jae-Hyun Baek1,2 Byung-Sun Won3 Jon-Lark Kim4,2∗ 1 Department of Artificial Intelligence, Sogang University, Seoul, Korea 2 Institute for Mathematical and Data Sciences, Sogang University, Seoul, Korea 3 Ewha Institute of Mathematical Sciences, Ewha Womans University, Seoul, Korea 4 Department of Mathematics, Sogang University, Seoul, Korea arXiv:2610.41183v1 [cs.AI] 30 Oct 2026 A BSTRACT LLM-guided program evolution can produce mathematical constructions, but va- lidity, generality, and reproducibility require distinct evidence. We develop a researcher-in-the-loop discovery pipeline that combines program evolution, ex- act evaluation, mathematical generalization, certified nonexistence checks, and formal proof checking. We apply it to entanglement-assisted quantum error- correcting codes (EAQECCs). Starting from tasks that did not specify a family formula, evolved programs produced finite qubit constructions whose structure researchers generalized to the family [[n, 1, n − 1; n − q − 1]]q for prime powers q ≥ 3 at n ≥ 2q + 1 and for q = 2 at odd n ≥ 5. Lean checks the algebraic certifi- cate underlying this family. Together with entanglement lifting, the family closes 54 gaps in archived EAQECC tables. The released evidence includes 115 verified code records, ten nonexistence results with checked DRAT proofs, family imple- mentations, and preserved search programs for exact checks and seeded replay. In a controlled cohort of eight paired generation blocks, validation-selected iterative programs achieve success in 46.1% and 31.6% of held-out executions at unseen lengths n = 13, 15, compared with 19.5% and 3.1% for independently generated programs. In this setting, program evolution and researcher analysis turn finite computational discoveries into a proved family with independently checkable ev- idence. 1 I NTRODUCTION LLM-guided program search has produced mathematical constructions and algorithms (Romera- Paredes et al., 2024; Novikov et al., 2025). Their outputs can also support general mathematical results through researcher analysis. This raises three questions: whether evolved programs produce valid codes, whether their structure can be generalized and proved to work beyond the searched cases, and whether the resulting constructions and preserved searches can be independently repro- duced. Addressing these questions requires records of the initial task, computational discoveries and subsequent mathematical analysis. We study this process for entanglement-assisted quantum error-correcting codes (EAQECCs). Early AlphaEvolve searches produced finite qubit codes whose structure led us to an infinite qubit family. Further mathematical generalization gives the prime-power construction and proof in Theorem 1. The initial instructions suggested directions such as cyclic shifts, but did not provide this family formula. Later instructions explicitly incorporated the discovered qubit family (Appendix B.3), allowing it to guide further searches. Our reproducibility contribution concerns these mathematical constructions and their computational evidence. The artifact supplies code matrices, family implementations, proofs, task specifications and preserved search programs. papers.title: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
papers.first_page: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents Zihua She Xiao Wang Department of Statistics, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN 47907, USA she8@purdue.edu, wangxiao@purdue.edu arXiv:2610.35596v1 [stat.CO] 26 Oct 2026 Abstract Papers in statistical theory rest on long proofs that few readers check line by line. We present KAPPA (Kit of Agents for Proof-checking Papers with a proof Assistant), open-source software that organizes language model agents, run by Claude Code, to translate the proofs of a LATEX paper into the proof assistant Lean 4 with its library Mathlib and check them there, result by result. Each numbered result receives one of four verdicts: verified unconditionally; verified conditionally, with every cited or unproved input stated as a named hypothesis; issue recorded, with its place in the paper and the side at fault; or unfinished, with the reason. The kit follows the paper’s own proof step by step, rather than finding a new one. Separate agents write and review, each statement is compared with the paper before it is proved and fingerprinted afterwards, and every verdict rests on evidence that can be rerun without a language model. The kit runs unattended for hours, waits out usage limits, re-checks only what a revision changed and reports its cost by role, model and result. We describe the design, walk through a complete run, and apply the kit to four example papers with answer keys and to three published statistical papers, checked blind in their versions from before public corrections. In all three, the kit found the published error at the step that the correction names, together with further problems that we confirmed by hand. Given the same papers directly, the same language model working with Lean classified fewer results correctly on the longest paper and reported some statements narrower than the paper’s as proved; no verdict of the kit claimed more than its Lean evidence showed. Keywords: proof checking, formal verification, Lean, language models, statistical theory, re- producibility. 1 Introduction A theorem in a statistics paper usually rests on a proof in an appendix, often several pages long, that combines a few cited results with many routine steps. Readers and referees follow the main line of the argument, and errors in the routine steps can go unnoticed. Journals publish corrections when such errors come to light (three recent ones are Henzi and Ziegel 2022a; Arab, Lando, and Oliveira 2026; Livingstone, Betancourt, Byrne, and Girolami 2026). Two of these three leave the theorem true and repair its proof, one corrects a false statement, and in each the error sits in a single step that a careful reader could have checked. A specialist can formalize such a result in a proof assistant such as Lean 4 (de Moura and Ullrich 2021) with the library Mathlib (The mathlib Community 2020), and a small trusted kernel then checks every step; formalizing one statistics paper in this way can take weeks of expert work. A language model reads a proof in minutes, but its answer is another informal argument that someone has to check. 1

papers.title: Hierarchical Skill Evolution for Coding Agent
papers.first_page: H IERARCHICAL S KILL E VOLUTION FOR C ODING AGENTS Jun Gao, Yun Peng, Changhai Zhou, Yuhan Zhu, Xiangyu Zeng, Shiyang Zhang Yuhua Zhou, Luozheng Qin, Qian Qiao, Xiaoteng Ma, Baian Chen Weiyi Shang, Zhen Ming Jack Jiang, Lizhi Liao, Xiaoxue Ren github.com/jungao1106/SKILL EVO A BSTRACT arXiv:2610.35616v1 [cs.CL] 26 Oct 2026 Skills provide agents with reusable experience to guide future decisions without modifying the underlying model. However, coding trajectories are often entan- gled with task- and repository-specific contexts, making it challenging to distill procedural skills that generalize across diverse coding environments. To address this challenge, we present Hierarchical Skill Evolution (HSE), which progres- sively distills procedural knowledge from coding trajectories through hierarchical evidence aggregation. HSE first extracts task-level evidence from individual tra- jectories, then aggregates recurring evidence within the same repository to form repository-specific skill candidates, and finally consolidates consistent patterns across repositories into transferable skills across repositories. The evolution is driven by an external writer–evaluator loop that generates and assesses skills while keeping the underlying coding model frozen. The loop externally updates the writer and evaluator policies to improve subsequent skill generation and assess- ment. This hierarchy progressively filters task-specific details while preserving procedures that generalize across diverse coding environments. Successful tra- jectories yield reusable guidance for future tasks, while failed trajectories reveal recurring failure modes that guide avoidance and recovery. We evaluate HSE on SWE-bench Verified and DeepSWE, using GLM-5.2 across Pi and Claude Code harnesses and GPT-5.5 an … for candidate assessment and achieving additional gains through benchmark-tailored skills. 1 I NTRODUCTION Skills allow coding agents to reuse experience from previous tasks without modifying the underly- ing model (Wang et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Ouyang et al., 2026b). This is particularly attractive for repository-level coding, where every attempt produces a rich trajec- tory of searches, code inspection, edits, tests, and recovery actions (Yang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025). Reusing these trajectories could prevent an agent from repeatedly rediscovering the same repair strategies. A trajectory, however, is not yet a reusable skill. It is entangled with a particular issue, repository structure, file paths, and patch, whereas a useful skill should guide future decisions without assuming that these task-specific details transfer. Existing forms of agent experience expose both sides of this problem. Raw trajectory retrieval pre- serves concrete evidence but can encourage agents to copy solutions that are specific to a previous task or repository (Chen et al., 2025). SWESkillsBench provides broadly applicable domain knowl- edge, but this guidance may not tell an agent how to localize a particular bug, constrain a patch, validate the affected behavior, or recover after an incorrect edit (Han et al., 2026). Methods that synthesize or optimize skills from trajectories demonstrate that experience can be converted into reusable instructions (Zhao et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Ouyang et al., 2026b; Ni et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026a; Agrawal et al., 2026), but a central challenge remains: at what level should evi- dence be aggregated so that task-specific details are removed without also discarding the procedure that made the experience useful? 1
